outline.title: Abstract
outline.description: A concise summary of the entire survey paper. It will outline the rapid evolution of LLM and MLLM security vulnerabilities from 2022 to 2026, highlighting the shift from isolated, modality-specific exploits to systemic, agentic, and protocol-level threats. The abstract will synthesize findings across four major threat vectors: data/model poisoning, prompt injection, adversarial attacks, and hallucinations, while emphasizing the critical need for standardized testing methodologies and holistic defense frameworks.

outline.title: Introduction
outline.description: This section establishes the motivation, scope, and contributions of the survey. It will introduce the paradigm shift in LLM security as models evolve from simple text-based chatbots to complex, multimodal autonomous agents. The introduction will map the trajectory of research from 2022 to 2026, noting how early foundational vulnerabilities have matured into sophisticated, automated exploits. It will outline the paper's structure, explicitly detailing how it covers the lifecycle of LLM threats from training-time (poisoning) to inference-time (prompt injection, adversarial attacks) and output-level failures (hallucinations).

outline.title: Background and Preliminaries
outline.description: Provides the foundational knowledge necessary to understand the subsequent sections. It will define key LLM and MLLM architectural components, including instruction tuning, alignment processes (RLHF, DPO), and multimodal integration (text, vision, code). This section will also establish a unified threat model taxonomy, categorizing attackers by their capabilities (white-box vs. black-box) and access points (training data, model weights, inference prompts, retrieved context).

outline.title: Training-Time Threats: Data and Model Poisoning
outline.description: Examines the chronological evolution of data and model poisoning, transitioning from early multimodal contrastive learning vulnerabilities (e.g., CLIP poisoning via malicious text-image pairs as seen in Yang_2022_Data) to sophisticated latent backdoors in modern LLMs. A major focus will be the 2024-2025 shift toward exploiting instruction-tuned models and the extreme fragility of alignment processes. It will detail how injecting merely 1-5% poisoned data can completely subvert RLHF and DPO guardrails, referencing key studies like Duan_2025_RLHF, Dutta_2025_RLHF, and Shi_2025_Safer. It will also cover emerging taxonomies for data, weight, and hidden state poisoning (Chen_2025_Survey, Chowdhury_2024_Breaking, Li_2024_Backdoorllm).

outline.title: Inference-Time Threats I: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
outline.description: Analyzes the trajectory of Prompt Injection (PI) from late 2023 to 2026. It will cover the foundational exploratory phase where researchers defined the problem space through manual red-teaming, utilizing taxonomies that separate 'Direct' attacks (payload splitting, virtualization) from 'Indirect' attacks (active/passive injections in retrieved data), as established by Rossi_2024_Early. The section will trace the evolution of these vulnerabilities as LLMs matured from isolated chatbots to autonomous, tool-using agents, highlighting how indirect prompt injection in RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) systems has exponentially expanded the attack surface.

outline.title: Inference-Time Threats II: Adversarial Attacks and Automated Exploits
outline.description: Explores the rapid sophistication of adversarial attacks on LLMs and MLLMs. It will begin with 2024 research focusing on foundational vulnerabilities, such as data poisoning in high-stakes medical LLMs (Yang_2024_Adversarial), visual noise/text injections in multimodal web agents (Wu_2024_Dissecting), and the fragility of code models (Hossen_2024_Adversarial, Rubel_2024_LLM). The section will then detail the critical 2025 paradigm shift towards automated, closed-loop attack generation and the exploitation of semantics-preserving transformations (SPTs) that systematically degrade model performance while evading basic filters.

outline.title: Output-Level Vulnerabilities: Hallucinations and Factual Inconsistencies
outline.description: Investigates the evolution of LLM hallucinations from 2023 to 2026. It will cover the shift from treating hallucinations as monolithic errors to understanding their nuanced behavioral dimensions. The section will discuss the categorization of hallucinations into distinct subtypes, specifically differentiating between errors where the model possesses the correct internal knowledge (HK+) versus lacking it (HK-) (Simhi_2024_LLM). It will also address the human perception of these errors, noting user struggles to detect minor fabrications (Nahar_2024_LLM), and the reframing of hallucinations not just as failures, but as inherent features of generative architectures requiring specialized trust and safety interventions.

outline.title: Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: Provides a holistic overview of defense mechanisms designed to secure LLMs across the identified threat vectors. It will discuss early 2024 defensive strategies such as prompt engineering and code-style structuring to mitigate textual attacks (Zhang_2024_Rocoins), and the use of stateful embedding banks for query detection (Wang_2024_Advqdet). The section will synthesize how defenses are evolving from isolated patches to systemic, protocol-level security architectures, including robust alignment techniques, input sanitization, retrieval-augmented verification, and continuous runtime monitoring.

outline.title: Testing Methodologies and Evaluation
outline.description: A mandatory, dedicated section synthesizing evaluation frameworks, benchmarks, and metrics across all threat categories. It will cover the transition from expensive human annotation to automated evaluation, highlighting milestones like the ChainPoll methodology and LLM-as-a-judge frameworks with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting for hallucination detection (Friel_2023_LLM). It will also detail standardized benchmarks for evaluating data/weight poisoning (Chen_2025_Survey, Chowdhury_2024_Breaking), and the shift from manual red-teaming (Rossi_2024_Early) to automated, scalable vulnerability scanning tools for prompt injection and adversarial attacks.

outline.title: Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: Critically analyzes the current state of LLM security research, identifying significant gaps and limitations in existing literature. It will discuss the ongoing 'cat-and-mouse' dynamic between attackers and defenders, the theoretical limits of alignment, and the unresolved challenges in securing autonomous, multi-agent systems. Future directions will be proposed, emphasizing the need for verifiable training pipelines, multimodal security guarantees, and the integration of psychological and behavioral insights into trust and safety frameworks.

outline.title: Conclusion
outline.description: Synthesizes the core findings of the survey, reiterating the rapid evolution of LLM vulnerabilities and the critical need for proactive, systemic security measures. It will provide actionable, practical recommendations for researchers, developers, and policymakers to foster the safe deployment of next-generation foundational models and autonomous agents.
